title: The young monk (373–382)
hook: rouse yourself by yourself; a young monk who applies himself lights up the world like the moon

segments.voice: Yesterday, empty the boat, and your line was the same: empty the boat. Which worry did you bail out? Day two hundred twenty-four, the end of the week and of the mendicant chapter.

You've probably met someone who does one thing with their whole heart. A kid practicing free throws in the driveway after dark. A cook who tastes the soup six times. A teenager learning a language on their own, just because they love it. There's a brightness about people like that. You notice it across a room. Nobody told them to. They roused themselves. The mendicant chapter ends with exactly that picture: someone young, wholehearted, and shining. Today: the young monk.
screen: `FREE THROWS AFTER DARK.` → `A BRIGHTNESS ACROSS A ROOM.` → `NOBODY TOLD THEM TO.`

segments.voice: The last verses of chapter twenty-five read like advice to a new monk. When you go into an empty room and sit, with a quiet heart, and see the teaching clearly, there's a joy beyond ordinary joys. Watching the body's pieces arise and pass away brings happiness, the text says. Guard the senses, be content, keep good friends. Then a lovely picture: as the jasmine drops its withered flowers, drop greed and hatred. Then the heart of the passage. Rouse yourself by yourself, the text says; examine yourself by yourself. You are your own protector, and your own refuge. Train yourself the way a merchant trains a good horse. And the chapter's last verse, three hundred eighty-two, in Max Müller's English: "He who, even as a young Bhikshu, applies himself to the doctrine of Buddha, brightens up this world, like the moon when free from clouds." The commentary connects it to a novice named Sumana, still a child, whom the Buddha praised. The point isn't age. It's that you don't have to wait until you're wise, or old, or finished, to shine. You shine by applying yourself, now. You've spent the week on thirst and its way out. The creeper of tanha, and digging up its root. The web you spun, and stepping out of it. The best gift, the teaching. Bhikkhu, and restraint of the senses. The emptied boat. Chapter twenty-five ends with a young monk lighting up the world, and tomorrow the last chapter begins.
screen: `JOY IN AN EMPTY ROOM.` · `DROP THEM LIKE WITHERED JASMINE.` · `ROUSE YOURSELF BY YOURSELF.` · `LIKE THE MOON FREE FROM CLOUDS.` · then, large: `YOUNG AND AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. For this sit, do one thing wholeheartedly: breathe. Not halfway, while planning dinner. Give each breath your whole attention, the way the kid gives it to the free throw. Feel it begin, feel it fill, feel it turn, feel it leave. When the mind wanders, rouse yourself, by yourself, with no scolding, and come back to the next breath, fresh, like a beginner. You are the young monk here. The bell holds the time.
The young monk. Rouse yourself by yourself: whoever applies themselves wholeheartedly brightens the world like the moon out of the clouds.
Your line: young and awake. Today, do one ordinary thing wholeheartedly, a dish, a walk, a conversation, like a beginner who loves it. Day two hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: In several Buddhist countries children may ordain as novices, sometimes for a few weeks or a season; teachers use verse 382 to encourage the young, and verses 379–380 to teach self-reliance in practice.

match.prompt: match each piece of today's verses.
pairs: brightens the world like the moon
a child novice in the commentary

myth: verse 382 says you must be old to shine
it praises a young monk who applies himself: brightness comes from effort, not age.
the verses call you your own protector and refuge
rouse yourself by yourself; examine yourself by yourself.
the jasmine image is about keeping every flower
as the jasmine drops its withered flowers, drop greed and hatred.

fork.setup: you're new to a practice and surrounded by people who've done it for decades. what do today's verses suggest?
options: wait until you're experienced to take it seriously.
fork.reveal: verse 382: even a young monk who applies himself brightens up the world like the moon when free from clouds.

original.note: Pali dahara: young; verse 382 speaks of the 'daharo bhikkhu', the young monk.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'the young monk' is only about children in robes.
what it means: anyone who rouses themselves and applies themselves wholeheartedly shines, at any age.
what a scholar hears: 'yo have daharo bhikkhu yunjati buddhasasane'; the commentary ties it to the novice Sumana, and verse 380 says 'atta hi attano natho', self is the lord of self.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
